claim: The retrieved archaeometric literature names at least eleven lapis lazuli deposits worldwide and treats at least seven as candidate ancient sources: Sar-e Sang (Badakhshan, Afghanistan), Lyadjuar Dara (Tajikistan), the Chagai Hills (Pakistan), Lake Baikal (Siberia), the Urals, Ovalle (Chile) and Mogok (Myanmar). Ariccia (Italy), North America, Canada and Vesuvius are also named.
locator: SRC-107 Introduction, chunk 1 ('There are mainly 11 deposits of lapis lazuli that have been found around the world'); SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunks 14-15; SRC-108 INTRODUCTION chunk 1
notes: VERIFIED as a statement of what these publications say. The count of eleven is attributed by SRC-107 to its reference [16], which is not in the retrieved passages and cannot be checked here; the proposition 'there are eleven deposits in the world' is therefore not itself verified. This claim is the first half of the owner's first trap: the alternatives to Badakhshan exist, are named in print, and are numerous.

claim: The most recent analytical protocol named in the retrieved literature discriminates among four sampled provenances only - Ovalle (Chile), Lyadjuar Dara (Tajikistan), Badakhshan (Afghanistan) and Lake Baikal (Siberia) - which is fewer than the number of candidate ancient sources at DRB-001.
locator: SRC-106 chunk 14: 'The protocol was based on the study and analysis of four main provenances: Ovalle (Chile), Liadjura-Dara or Lojvar Dara (Tajikistan), Badakhshan (Afghanistan) and Lake Baikal (Siberia)', citing Lo Giudice et al. 2017 and Guidorzi et al. 2023
notes: Read together with DRM-002 this is the whole of the first trap. A protocol built on four sampled sources can only ever return one of those four. Chagai, Mogok, Ariccia, the Urals and the North American occurrences are not in it, so an object from any of them would be assigned to whichever of the four it most resembles.

claim: The three published discriminating markers are stated as exclusions rather than identifications: absence of wollastonite indicates Tajikistan, Afghanistan or Siberia; absence of altered pyrite and of Sr in diopside indicates Tajikistan or Afghanistan; a higher Ni/Cu ratio in pyrite indicates Afghanistan (Badakhshan).
locator: SRC-106 chunk 13, the three bulleted markers, citing Guidorzi et al. 2023 and Lo Giudice et al. 2017
notes: Only the third marker is stated positively, and only it distinguishes Afghanistan from Tajikistan. The first two narrow a field of four to three and then to two. A published protocol whose discriminating power rests on one ratio in one mineral phase is a thinner instrument than the phrase 'chemical fingerprint' suggests.

claim: Lapis provenance studies are, in the field's own summary, 'extensively debated but not solved', and most have focused on the Sar-e Sang deposits while 'rarely considering the close exploitable sources in Pakistan and Tajikistan'.
locator: SRC-108 INTRODUCTION chunk 1
notes: A statement about the distribution of research attention, published inside the field, in Archaeometry. It is the mechanism behind the trap rather than an accusation about it: Badakhshan is best characterised partly because it has been studied most, and being best characterised makes it the most available match.

claim: The Chagai Hills are retained as a candidate lapis source in the literature although the deposit's existence is doubted; as reported, Law 2014 holds it 'neither documented nor supported by geological data' and suggests that rock samples associated with Chagai came from the Badakhshan quarries.
locator: SRC-106 chunk 14
notes: Chagai is the principal rival to Badakhshan for the eastern Iranian plateau material, and it is the one whose reference samples are said to be misattributed Badakhshan.

claim: In the retrieved reasoning, the elimination of Chagai as a distinct source proceeds by re-attributing its reference samples to Badakhshan, after which Badakhshan becomes the most probable source: 'If the Chagai's data might be more likely from Badakhshan, then Badakhshan (and especially Sar-e Sang) is the most probably rock resource for the Iranian Plateau.'
locator: SRC-106 chunk 14, final sentence
notes: Recorded as a description of an inferential structure, not as an accusation of error. The re-attribution has a stated evidential basis - sulphur-isotope overlap between the Chagai Hills samples and Afghan ones - and may well be right. What the record notes is the shape of the consequence: the rival source is removed by reassigning its reference material to the favoured source, and the reference set then contains one fewer alternative for every future study. That is how a field converges, and it is also how a field can converge on a wrong answer, and nothing retrieved here distinguishes the two cases.

claim: The Persepolis object data and the reference data they are compared with are not method-commensurable: the objects were powdered and measured by WD-XRF, the reference set was measured by PGAA on whole rock without pre-treatment, and the authors themselves attribute the observed divergence to that difference rather than to source.
locator: SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunk 13: 'The reason of variation of Persepolitan samples with different sources could be due to the process of analysis used by Zoldfoldi and Kasztovszky ... as they used PGAA on whole rock without pretreatment while the Persepolitan samples are completely powdered and analysed by WDXRF'
notes: This is stated by the authors and is the strongest single reason not to promote DRB-010 above PROVISIONAL. When the object plots outside every reference cluster and the explanation offered is instrumental, the comparison has not been made.

claim: A 2025 study assessing the Persepolis work holds that its mineralogical characterisation 'was not very informative for provenance, as the Asian lapis lazuli sources that are generally taken into account do not show significant differences in their mineralogy'.
locator: SRC-107 Introduction chunk 5
notes: The next paper to cite the Persepolis study downgrades its central instrument. Recorded under step 11, current standing: the strongest published claim on this material is not the field's settled reading of it two years later.

claim: A companion study of four lapis pieces from the Bronze Age stone-working workshop at Konar Sandal South (Jiroft plain, Iran) 'produced inconclusive results when compared to data from reference rock samples obtained in other studies using PIXE'.
locator: SRC-107 Introduction chunk 5
notes: A second instance of DRB-007's problem, at a different site and with a different technique pairing (SEM-EDS against PIXE). Cross-technique comparison against other laboratories' reference data is where these studies fail, and it fails twice in the retrieved record.

claim: That the lapis of the five Persepolis cylinders came from Badakhshan.
locator: SRC-106 CONCLUSIONS chunk 16 and RESULTS chunk 14
notes: One study; its reference comparison is method-incommensurable by its own account (DRB-007); its mineralogy is judged uninformative by the next paper to use it (DRB-008); its rival source was eliminated by reassignment (DRB-006); and the supplementary data behind the pyrite Ni/Cu marker were not delivered by the passage-level lane (SRC-105). The Ni/Cu marker is the one line of evidence not so qualified, and it is why this is PROVISIONAL rather than HYPOTHESIS. Not promotable without the article and its figures.

claim: The Persepolis study states, in the same article, both that 'the available data are not sufficient to prove their origin' and that a finding 'proves that the Persepolitan lapis lazuli objects share a provenance with others from Afghanistan (Badakhshan)'.
locator: SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunk 11 ('Although the present study shows a probable trade ... the available data are not sufficient to prove their origin'), chunk 12 (the same sentence repeated as a standalone), and chunk 14 ('Accordingly, this finding proves that ...')
notes: A textual observation about one article, recorded and not adjudicated. Both sentences were retrieved. The unit does not claim the authors contradicted themselves in substance - the first sentence concerns the trace-element comparison and the third concerns the pyrite Ni/Cu ratio, and those are different evidence - but the article's own summary language moves from insufficiency to proof within a few pages, and a reader taking only the conclusion would carry away the second and not the first. That gap is how a PROVISIONAL result becomes a citable certainty downstream, which is the mechanism step 11 exists to catch.

claim: That the lapis worked at Shahr-i Sokhta came from Badakhshan.
locator: SRC-106 chunks 11, 12, 13, citing Casanova 1992, Casanova 1998 and Law 2014
notes: The retrieved account is internally divided. Casanova's atomic-absorption Ba/Sr data place the majority of Shahr-i Sokhta samples with Sar-e Sang, Badakhshan and Pamir but relate others to Chagai; SRC-106 chunk 11 reports the earlier reading that the provenance 'may be more likely from Chagai (Pakistan)'; the sulphur-isotope evidence for Badakhshan is reported as resting on ONE sample from the site. One sample is not a provenance for a site with, on the same source's account, large-scale bead production.

claim: SRC-106 reports that Darius's foundation charter for the Apadana at Susa (DSf), written in Old Persian, Akkadian and Elamite, names Sogdiana - not Badakhshan - as the place from which lapis lazuli and carnelian were brought.
locator: SRC-106 RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS chunk 15, citing Basello 2012 and Kent 1953
notes: The clearest case in this unit of a textual provenance label that is not a geological source and must not be read as one. Whether or not that reconciliation is right, the inscription states who supplied, not where the rock formed, and those are two of the owner's ten fields. | REWORDED for status discipline: what is VERIFIED is that the named source states this, with the locator given. claim: The inference underlying every provenance claim on both roads is Damour's of 1865 - that an object whose material is foreign to the region implies transport of the object or of the matter it is made from - and it 'has essentially gone unchallenged since 1865'.
locator: SRC-121 chunk 1, quoting Damour 1865: 313 in French with an English translation
notes: The dated warrant behind the whole domain, and the reason the three-claim rule is not a stylistic preference. Damour's inference licenses a conclusion about the movement of matter and about nothing else. Every step from matter to people, and from people to language, is an additional inference that Damour does not supply and that must be evidenced separately. BR-R-001 to BR-R-003.

claim: Canonical discriminant analysis 'assumes that the dataset being evaluated contains all possible groups', so an artefact 'will be assigned membership in the group it most closely resembles even if the group (source) to which it actually belongs is not present in the dataset'.
locator: SRC-109 EVALUATION OF THE RESULTS, chunk 13, final paragraph
notes: Stated by the analysts themselves, about their own method. This is the general form of the owner's first trap and it governs both roads: an unsampled source is not a weak match, it is invisible, and its objects are silently distributed among the sources that were sampled. Read with DRB-002 it means that a four-source lapis protocol cannot report 'none of these'.

claim: Increasing the density of geological sampling is expected to REDUCE the apparent separation between sources, not improve it; the authors of one reference dataset 'anticipated that additional geochemical data from geological samples would probably lead to more overlaps between sources'.
locator: SRC-122 DISCUSSION
notes: The counter-intuitive half of DRM-002, and the more dangerous one. Apparent discrimination between sources can be an artefact of thin sampling, so a protocol that separates four lapis sources cleanly is not thereby shown to be a good instrument; it may be showing the gaps in its own reference set. The same passage adds that geological samples collected to answer geological questions cannot simply be reused as provenance comparison material, because the sampling criteria differ.

claim: In the wider sourcing literature 'some artefacts reported in the literature have been assigned to quarries based on one published geochemical analysis for a particular source', and source characterisations built on second-hand collections rather than field sampling carry Type I and Type II error risks the analyst 'may not even be aware' of.
locator: SRC-123 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS; SRC-124 'The chemical characterization of stone: beyond fishing expeditions'
notes: Both statements are about lithic sourcing generally - Polynesian basalt and North American chert - and neither is about lapis or carnelian. Carried as general statements about the practice and labelled as such, because they name the exact conditions the lapis reference sets meet: small samples, and museum or merchant material standing in for field collection (DRR-004).

claim: SRC-126 reports that beads from the third-millennium stone-working workshop at Konar Sandal (Jiroft) previously 'identified as calcite' on the artefacts' appearance were shown by micro-Raman, micro-XRF, FTIR and XRD to be gypsum alabaster - a material attribution made from appearance, overturned by analysis.
locator: SRC-126 abstract and Discussion
notes: The plainest available demonstration that the museum-candidate register's material column is a hypothesis and not a datum. The underlying proposition about the world was not independently checked here and, on a single source, would be PROVISIONAL at best.

claim: Of 863 texts in the CDLI corpus naming at least one of Meluhha, Magan, Dilmun and Marhashi, 813 - 94.2% - name exactly one; 39 name two, 10 name three, and one text names all four.
locator: 04-AUDITS/domain-r-cdli-distributions.py, CO-OCCURRENCE section, over 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv; the four-name text is P469516, catalogued Old Babylonian, provenience Nippur
notes: The owner's fourth trap answered with a number rather than an assurance. The four are, in the surviving record, overwhelmingly named apart. Pairwise: Magan with Meluhha in 38 texts, Dilmun with Magan in 12, Dilmun with Meluhha in 11, Marhashi with Meluhha in 9, Dilmun with Marhashi in 3, Magan with Marhashi in 2. The familiar triad of Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha - which is how modern synthesis almost always introduces them - stands in nine of 863 texts. Marhashi is the most separate of the four.

claim: The sign sequence me-luh-ha carries at least four different determinatives in the corpus and stands in at least five functions: the land determinative {kur}, the place determinative {ki}, the bird determinative {muszen} in the lexical bird name dar-meluhha, wood terms (mes-me-luh-ha, ab-ba-me-luh-ha), and the personal-name element in dumu me-luh-ha.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv, target MELUHHA: 67 LAND-DETERMINATIVE, 20 PLACE-DETERMINATIVE, 4 BIRD-DETERMINATIVE (P228354, P229306, P231266, P247815, all reading dar me-luh-ha{muszen}), 23 BOUND-IN-COMPOUND-OR-NAME (11 mes-me-luh-ha, 7 ab-ba-me-luh-ha)
notes: A textual provenance label is not one kind of thing. The same sequence names a land, a place, a bird, two timbers and a person. Reading every occurrence as a reference to a region overstates the toponym by roughly a quarter of its occurrences, and the wood and bird uses are the ones a materials domain is most likely to mistake for evidence of trade in a material.

claim: The determinative on Meluhha shifts with period. In third-millennium and Old Babylonian texts it takes the place determinative {ki} - 20 occurrences, none with {kur} - and appears in granary and personnel records, chiefly at Girsu. In Neo-Assyrian texts it takes the land determinative {kur} - 67 occurrences, none with {ki} - and appears in royal itineraries and titulature, chiefly at Nineveh.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv, target MELUHHA, cross-tabulated by cdli_period; representative Ur III lines i3-dub me-luh-ha (P100892, P102031) and e2-duru5-me-luh-ha{ki} (P108484); representative Neo-Assyrian lines a-na {kur}ma2-kan-na u {kur}me-luh-ha lu-u al-lik (P392229) and _lugal_ {kur}me-luh-ha (P392594)
notes: A measured orthographic change accompanying a change of genre and of place of writing, across roughly 1,400 years. This unit does NOT assert what the Neo-Assyrian word denotes; it records that the referent cannot be assumed constant, and that a corridor argument built on 'Meluhha' must say which Meluhha it means. The standard identification of the first-millennium term with Nubia is not retrieved here and is not asserted; HOLD-009.

claim: The four labels did not survive equally into the first millennium. Marhashi has 1 first-millennium text against 152 earlier; Dilmun 14 against 232; Magan 33 against 328; Meluhha 55 against 110.
locator: 04-AUDITS/domain-r-cdli-distributions.py period tables over 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv
notes: Meluhha is by a wide margin the most reused of the four: a third of its texts are first-millennium, against under one per cent for Marhashi. Which labels remained available for later imperial rhetoric is a fact about the archive and its makers, not about the places. It is also why Meluhha carries more accumulated interpretation than the other three and needs more care, not less.

claim: Every findspot for the four toponyms in this corpus is in Mesopotamia, Syria or Assyria - Girsu, Nineveh, Ur, Nippur, Puzrish-Dagan, Umma, Adab, Assur, Ebla, Shuruppak. No text naming Meluhha, Magan, Dilmun or Marhashi in this corpus was found in the Indus region, Gujarat, Oman, Bahrain or Iran.
locator: 04-AUDITS/domain-r-cdli-distributions.py PROVENIENCE tables over 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv
notes: The archive audit in one measurement. The entire textual provenance record for both roads was written at one end of the corridor, by the importing societies, about the exporting ones. Meluhha is a word in someone else's language for somewhere else, and there is no surviving text from the place it names. Typed at DR-NEG-001. This is a property of THIS corpus, which is a Mesopotamian-focused publication; the constraint is stated at APA-R-001 rather than presented as a fact about the ancient world.

claim: Individuals designated dumu me-luh-ha, 'son of Meluhha', in Ur III records bear Sumerian names formed on Sumerian deities, among them Ur-Lamma and Ur-Ig-alim.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv, target MELUHHA: ki ur-{d}lamma dumu me-luh-ha-ta (P102519), ur-{d}lamma dumu me-luh-ha (P108448), x ur-{d}ig-alim dumu me-luh-ha (P124739), kiszib3 ur-{d}lamma dumu me-luh-ha (P136196); 14 occurrences in 12 texts, all catalogued Ur III
notes: Directly on the owner's three-claim rule and retrieved from the primary corpus rather than argued. Whether dumu me-luh-ha is an ethnic designation or a patronymic on a personal name Meluhha is not settled by the phrase, and both readings are live. Under either, the name actually borne is Sumerian and theophoric. A person carrying a foreign toponym as a designation is not thereby a speaker of a foreign language, and this is the case in the record where that can be seen rather than assumed. BR-R-003.

claim: That the modern site name Mehrgarh is evidence of identity with the cuneiform toponym Marhashi.
locator: No source proposing the identification was retrieved; the corpus evidence for the toponym is 03-REGISTERS/domain-r-cdli-attestations.csv target MARHASI, 153 texts, written mar-ha-szi{ki} and variants mar-ha-s,i and mar-ha-s,u
notes: Rejected as an inference, and the row is kept so it is not re-proposed. Recording the rejection is not a finding about where Marhashi was, which this unit could not retrieve and holds at HOLD-009.

notes: A chronology-gate finding. Any Blue Road argument that dates a lapis workshop by reference to a Shahr-i Sokhta phase inherits a five-century uncertainty, and most such arguments do not state it.

claim: The equations Meluhha = the Indus Valley, Magan = Oman and south-east Arabia, Dilmun = Bahrain and the adjacent Arabian coast, and Marhashi = south-eastern Iran are carried in the current literature as settled parentheses rather than as argued claims.
locator: SRC-117 abstract ('southern Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley (Meluhha), southeast Iran (Marhashi) and Bahrain (Dilmun)'); SRC-109 INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND chunk 3, citing Laursen and Steinkeller 2017 and Leemans 1960; SRC-112 chunk 3, citing Weisgerber 1981a and Potts 1990
notes: The identifications may well be correct and this unit does not contest them. What it records is their form in the literature: a parenthesis after a toponym, referred to a small number of upstream authorities, in papers whose own evidence is ceramic or metallurgical and not toponymic. Under the source-independence rule the recurrence of the equation across many papers is not many confirmations of it. DEP-029.

claim: Magan's identification with Oman rests substantially on material rather than on toponymic evidence: the argument named in the retrieved literature is that third- and second-millennium cuneiform tablets repeatedly mention copper and black stone in connection with Magan, and lead-isotope analysis places a considerable quantity of mid-third-millennium Mesopotamian copper in Omani sources.
locator: SRC-112 chunk 3, citing Weisgerber 1981a and Heimpel 1987: 69; SRC-113 chunk 4, citing Begemann and Schmitt-Strecker 2009: 24
notes: Recorded because it is the one of the four identifications with an independent physical check, and because that check is of the same kind this domain is auditing. It is also the case where the same authors' further inference - that a purer copper originated in Gujarat and reached Mesopotamia via Bahrain - is described in the retrieved literature as remaining 'to be verified from others sources'.

claim: Fifteen carnelian beads from Burial A51 on Mound A at Kish were analysed by LA-ICP-MS against a database of 25 agate-carnelian sources; all fifteen have both first and second predicted group membership in Deccan Traps deposits, and in the ten-source Deccan analysis ten have a first assignment to Ratanpur and four to Mardak Beyt, both in Gujarat.
locator: SRC-109 EVALUATION OF THE RESULTS, chunks 14 and 15
notes: VERIFIED as what the study reports. The supplementary appendices carrying the per-bead assignments were not delivered by the passage-level lane, so the numbers are the authors' summary of their own tables, not a reading of the tables.

claim: The cross-validation of that source database reclassifies 279 of 399 geological samples correctly, a leave-one-out success rate of 69.9%; of the 120 misclassified, all but 24 were assigned to another source within the same region, giving a regional success rate of 93.9%.
locator: SRC-109 EVALUATION OF THE RESULTS, chunk 14
notes: The honest number and the reason the Kish result should be read regionally and not as a mine. The study says so itself. A source-level assignment from a method that misplaces three geological samples in ten is a regional statement wearing a specific name, and Ratanpur should be read as 'Gujarat' rather than as a quarry.

claim: Reducing the comparison from 25 sources to the 10 Deccan Traps sources barely changed the cross-validation rate, from 69.4% to 69.5%, because most misclassification is between sources within one regional terrain rather than between regions.
locator: SRC-109 EVALUATION OF THE RESULTS, chunk 15
notes: This is the finding that makes DRR-001 defensible at the regional level and undermines it at the source level, and the authors state both.

claim: The comparative source database averages about 17 analyses per source against a target of 20, and some of its sources are proxies rather than field-collected: archaeological bead-making debris standing for a nearby deposit (Tayma, Saudi Arabia), and samples bought from stone merchants (Sanaa in Yemen, Chalcedon and Ankara in Turkey).
locator: SRC-109 BUILDING A DATABASE OF POTENTIAL AGATE-CARNELIAN SOURCES, chunks 10 and 11
notes: Disclosed by the authors, who call the practice 'less than optimal' and intend it to be temporary. Recorded here because of where the proxies fall: the Arabian and Anatolian entries - the alternatives to India for a Mesopotamian bead - are the weakest-sampled in the set, so the comparison is strongest exactly where it favours the Indian sources and weakest where it would not.

claim: SRC-110 reports that Jebel al-Ma'taradh in Ra's al-Khaimah, in the region conventionally identified as Magan, holds carnelian, agate, chalcedony and chrysoprase deposits exploited from at least the seventh millennium BC, and records that before this work it was held that 'no geological source of chalcedony, agate, or carnelian has been identified up to now on the Arabian coast of the Gulf'.
locator: SRC-110 abstract chunk 0 and DISCUSSION chunks 7 and 8
notes: The owner's 'alternative geological sources' in their sharpest form, and a documented instance of an absence created by not having surveyed. On the earlier reading, Gulf Neolithic carnelian beads had to have been traded from Mesopotamia or Iran; on the present reading there is a source 30 to 50 km away. Typed at DR-NEG-004 as NOT RECOGNISED. | REWORDED for status discipline: what is VERIFIED is that the named source states this, with the locator given. The underlying proposition about the world was not independently checked here and, on a single source, would be PROVISIONAL at best.

claim: Bronze Age carnelian beads in United Arab Emirates museum collections show the mixed white-and-yellow veining observed in situ at Jebel al-Ma'taradh, which the excavators read as implying local production of such ornaments in the Bronze Age.
locator: SRC-110 DISCUSSION chunk 8
notes: The identification is macroscopic - veining seen by eye - not analytical, and the paper says no bead workshop has been found at the deposit itself. Recorded because if it holds, an Umm an-Nar carnelian bead is not by that fact an Indus product, which is the assumption the Red Road most often makes.

claim: All fifteen Kish beads were perforated with constricted cylindrical drills of the type designated Ernestite, a distinctively Indus technology, but four of them (beads 1, 6, 13 and 15) have ends chipped and only partly smoothed rather than ground flat as Indus finishing requires, and the bleached white designs on two of those are of lower quality than the Indus-standard examples in the same necklace.
locator: SRC-109 CARNELIAN BEADS FROM KISH, IRAQ, chunks 6 and 7
notes: The single most useful observation in this unit, because one necklace separates four of the owner's ten fields at once. Same geological source, same manufacturing tradition, same drilling technology, and two different standards of workshop execution. The study's own reading is that these beads were either part-finished in the Indus and completed in Mesopotamia, or made in Mesopotamia by craftspeople using Indus tools and techniques.

claim: The study's conclusion is that Indus craftspeople settled in Mesopotamian cities and produced, or taught others to produce, beads of Indus shape and decoration for local consumers, using imported raw material and some imported tools.
locator: SRC-109 CONCLUSIONS chunk 16
notes: A claim about people inferred from a claim about objects, and it is the exact junction the owner's rule polices. The evidence establishes an Indus technological repertoire operating in Mesopotamia. Whether the hands were Indus hands, hands taught by them, or hands that acquired the tools some other way is not settled by drill-hole morphology, and the study's own phrase 'or taught others to make' concedes the alternative. Tested at BR-R-002.

claim: SRC-109 states that carnelian of bead quality is generally a human-modified product: iron-rich agate is heated, in a process documented at Khambhat in Gujarat, to oxidise the iron and produce the red-orange colour, and that naturally heated carnelians tend to be cracked and harder to work.
locator: SRC-109 AGATE-CARNELIAN, chunk 7
notes: Bears on the field schema: the colour that names the material is a product of the manufacturing tradition, not of the geological source. claim: Results of LA-ICP-MS carnelian analysis are not currently comparable between laboratories, unlike glass compositions; a protocol for cross-laboratory comparison is described as under development.
locator: SRC-109 CONCLUSIONS chunk 16
notes: Every carnelian provenance result in the literature is therefore internal to the instrument that produced it, and a second laboratory cannot check the first. This is a source-independence fact, not a technical footnote: it means the Kish result has, and can presently have, no independent replication. DEP-030.
